proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(S\in\mathcal I\), put \(U=V\setminus S\) and \(O=X\setminus S\), and write \(A=Q^{-1}\), so \(C=A_{X,:}\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:regime\text{-}solvability}\) gives the inverse of \(Q_{U,U}\), while the empty-block convention gives determinant one when \(U=\varnothing\).  In the order \((S,U)\), block elimination gives
\[
\det Q=\det(Q_{U,U})\det\!\left(Q_{S,S}-Q_{S,U}Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}\right)
\]
and
\[
A_{S,S}=\left(Q_{S,S}-Q_{S,U}Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Both determinants on the first display are nonzero by regime solvability at \(S\) and at \(\varnothing\).  Consequently
\[
\det(C_{S,S})=\det(A_{S,S})
=\frac{\det(Q_{U,U})}{\det Q}\neq0.                                      \tag{3}
\]

The \((U,S)\) block of \(QA=I_N\) gives
\[
A_{U,S}=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}A_{S,S}.
\]
Since \(Q_{U,S}=-B_{U,S}\), restriction to the rows \(O\) and multiplication by \(A_{S,S}^{-1}\) yield
\[
T_S(C)=C_{O,S}C_{S,S}^{-1}
=\bigl[Q_{U,U}^{-1}B_{U,S}\bigr]_{O,:}.                                 \tag{4}
\]
The \((U,U)\) block of \(QA=I_N\), together with the preceding identity, also yields
\[
A_{U,U}-Q_{U,U}^{-1}B_{U,S}A_{S,U}=Q_{U,U}^{-1}.
\]
Thus the matrix \(R_S(C)=C_{O,:}-T_S(C)C_{S,:}\) has zero columns on \(S\) and equals \((Q_{U,U}^{-1})_{O,:}\) on \(U\).

Under the surgical intervention in \(\mathrm{ass:perfect\text{-}intervention}\), the remaining equations are
\[
Q_{U,U}V_U=\varepsilon_U+B_{U,S}x.
\]
Equations (3)--(4) therefore imply, on the structural probability space,
\[
X_O^{\operatorname{do}(X_S=x)}
=R_S(C)\varepsilon+T_S(C)x,
\]
and hence
\[
K_S^{B,\varepsilon}(x)=\mathcal L\bigl(R_S(C)\varepsilon+T_S(C)x\bigr).   \tag{5}
\]
Observationally, \(X=C\varepsilon\), so direct substitution gives
\[
R_S(C)\varepsilon=X_O-T_S(C)X_S.                                        \tag{6}
\]
Centering and finite first moments, supplied by source centering and the finite-second-moment restriction in the model class, give \(\mathbb E K_S(x)=T_S(C)x\).  Hence the kernel means at zero and at the unit coordinate values identify every entry of \(T_S(C)\); (6) identifies the residual law from the observational law, and (5) then identifies the entire affine kernel.  Finally, if \(C_{:,i}=0\), then the definition of \(R_S\) gives \(R_S(C)_{:,i}=0\) for every \(S\), proving that an observationally invisible source cannot become visible after an allowed intervention.  All arguments also cover \(S=\varnothing\), \(O=\varnothing\), and zero residual columns by the stated empty-matrix conventions.

Let \(P_X=[I_n\;0]\) denote the row selector from \(\mathbb R^V\) to \(\mathbb R^X\).  For the forward implication, suppose \(Q=I_N-B\) is admissible and \(C=P_XQ^{-1}\).  Then
\[
CQ=P_X.                                                                  \tag{7}
\]
The \(j\)-th column \(q_j\) of \(Q\) has diagonal coordinate one and has, away from that coordinate, a nonzero entry precisely at every child of \(j\), by exact support and looplessness.  Taking column \(j\) in (7) gives
\[
C_{:,j}+C_{:,\operatorname{ch}_G(j)}w=p_j,
\]
so \(q_j\in\mathcal A_j^\times(C)\).

We record why the displayed rank tests are exactly local punctured feasibility.  For a matrix \(M\), vector \(u\), and coordinate \(k\), the system \(Mw=u\) is soluble exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}M=\operatorname{rank}[M,u]\).  On a nonempty solution affine space, coordinate \(w_k\) is not identically zero precisely in either of the following mutually exhaustive cases: the deleted column belongs to the span of the remaining columns, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}M_{-k}=\operatorname{rank}M\); or that column increases rank, in which case \(w_k\) is uniquely determined and is nonzero precisely when \(u\notin\operatorname{col}(M_{-k})\), equivalently
\[
\operatorname{rank}[M_{-k},u]>\operatorname{rank}M_{-k}.                 \tag{8}
\]
A finite union of proper affine hyperplanes cannot cover a nonempty real affine space: after an affine parametrization, the product of their nonzero defining affine polynomials is a nonzero polynomial, and induction on the number of variables supplies a point where it is nonzero.  Thus (8) for every child coordinate is equivalent to \(\mathcal A_j^\times(C)\neq\varnothing\), including the zero-dimensional and empty-child cases.

Equation (7) and invertibility of \(Q\) imply \(\operatorname{rank}C=n\).  The latent columns \((q_j)_{j\in L}\) are linearly independent and belong to \(W_j(C)\), so every subfamily \(J\subseteq L\) satisfies
\[
\dim\left(\sum_{j\in J}W_j(C)\right)\geq |J|.                           \tag{9}
\]
Finally, the block determinant calculation (3) gives \(\det(C_{S,S})\neq0\) for every \(S\in\mathcal I\).  Hence \(C\in\mathcal D_G\).

Conversely, suppose \(C\in\mathcal D_G\).  The local tests and the preceding equivalence make every \(\mathcal A_j^\times(C)\) nonempty.  Apply the cited independent-transversal theorem to (9) to obtain independent \(v_j\in W_j(C)\), \(j\in L\).  Each \(v_j\) is a finite linear combination of points of \(\mathcal A_j(C)\).  A nonzero exterior product \(\bigwedge_{j\in L}v_j\), expanded multilinearly, therefore contains a nonzero term \(\bigwedge_{j\in L}q_j^0\) with \(q_j^0\in\mathcal A_j(C)\).  Equivalently, at least one \(\ell\)-row minor of the matrix of latent columns is a polynomial on \(\prod_{j\in L}\mathcal A_j(C)\) that is not identically zero.

For every graph edge \(j\to k\), the coordinate function \(q_j\mapsto(q_j)_k\) is also not identically zero on \(\mathcal A_j(C)\), by (8).  After affine parametrization of all fibers, the product of the selected independence minor and all these coordinate functions is a nonzero polynomial, since a real polynomial ring is an integral domain.  The elementary nonvanishing argument used above selects latent columns
\[
q_j\in\mathcal A_j^\times(C),\quad j\in L,                              \tag{10}
\]
that are linearly independent.  This chooses an actual point for the fixed \(C\); it makes no genericity assertion about \(C\) and takes no closure.

Choose any \(q_j\in\mathcal A_j^\times(C)\) for each observed \(j\), and stack all chosen columns as \(Q\).  By construction, \(Cq_j=p_j\), so \(CQ=P_X\).  If \(\sum_{j\in V}\lambda_jq_j=0\), applying \(C\) gives \(\sum_{j\in X}\lambda_je_j=0\), hence all observed coefficients vanish; (10) then makes all latent coefficients vanish.  Thus \(Q\) is invertible and
\[
C=P_XQ^{-1}.                                                             \tag{11}
\]
Every diagonal coordinate of \(Q\) is one, every off-diagonal coordinate not corresponding to an edge is zero, and every edge coordinate is nonzero.  Therefore \(B=I_N-Q\) has exact support \(G\).  For every \(S\in\mathcal I\), Jacobi's principal-minor identity, proved here by the same Schur-complement calculation as (3), gives
\[
\det Q_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S}=\det Q\,\det (Q^{-1})_{S,S}
=\det Q\,\det C_{S,S}\neq0.                                           \tag{12}
\]
Thus all required regimes are solvable.  Equations (10)--(12) construct the required exact-support mechanism, including all cancellation and lower-rank strata permitted by \(\mathcal D_G\).

Apply the finite-mixture containment lemma with \(A=C\) and the candidate matrix \(D\).  Its source class is exactly the class in the present statement: independence, centering, nonconstancy, non-Gaussianity, and finite second moments are each imposed coordinatewise, and zero mixing columns are handled by independent arbitrary legal sources.  The lemma gives
\[
\mathscr L(C)\subseteq\mathscr L(D)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists f:U_C\twoheadrightarrow U_D\ \exists(a_i)_{i\in U_C}\in(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})^{U_C}
\ \forall i\in U_C:\ C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}.
\]
Its necessity proof is the required diagnostic centered finite-support construction in the original free jump lattice \(\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z(r_iC_{:,i})\), and its Laurent factorization partitions rather than fractionally splits those generators.  Its sufficiency proof uses the same grouped source for every occurrence of a target column and proves, by the cited L\'evy--Cram\'er theorem, that each nonempty merged source remains non-Gaussian.  This proves both directions exactly, with invisible columns and source symmetries included.

We prove directed containment first.  Assume \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G)\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H)\), and fix \(C\in\mathcal D_G\).  By exact mixing realization, choose an exact-support admissible \(G\)-matrix \(Q\) whose observed mixing matrix is \(C\).  In the necessity construction of the finite-mixture containment lemma, choose the rationally independent centered Bernoulli jumps on the visible columns of \(C\), and arbitrary legal sources on its zero columns.  This produces a mechanism in the exact-support model class, hence a joint kernel tuple in \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G)\).  By containment the same tuple is generated by an admissible \(H\)-mechanism; let its observed mixing matrix be \(D\).  Exact mixing realization gives \(D\in\mathcal D_H\).

Equality of the empty-regime kernels gives \(\mathcal L(C\varepsilon)=\mathcal L(D\eta)\).  The diagnostic necessity argument in the finite-mixture lemma therefore supplies a surjection \(f:U_C\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero \(a_i\) with
\[
C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}.                                                    \tag{13}
\]
For any \(S\in\mathcal I\), source centering and finite first moments imply
\[
\mathbb E K_S(x)=T_S(C)x=T_S(D)x.
\]
Evaluating at the coordinate unit vectors of \(\mathbb R^S\) gives \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\); for \(S=\varnothing\) or \(X\setminus S=\varnothing\) this is the unique empty equality.  Thus all clauses of \(\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\) hold.

Conversely, assume the directed cover and take an arbitrary admissible \(G\)-mechanism with observed mixing matrix \(C\) and source vector \(\varepsilon\).  Exact mixing realization places \(C\) in \(\mathcal D_G\).  Choose the cover witness \((D,f,a)\).  The same theorem constructs an admissible exact-support \(H\)-matrix with observed mixing \(D\).  Define its visible sources by
\[
\eta_j=\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\varepsilon_i,\quad j\in U_D,                  \tag{14}
\]
and choose arbitrary independent centered nonconstant non-Gaussian finite-variance sources on the invisible columns.  Disjoint nonempty fibers make the variables in (14) independent; variance additivity proves nonconstancy and finite second moments; centering is linear; and L\'evy--Cram\'er proves non-Gaussianity.  Therefore this is an admissible common source tuple.  Equation (13) gives \(C\varepsilon=D\eta\).  Moreover, for every \(S\), equality of the response matrices and (13) imply columnwise
\[
R_S(C)_{:,i}=a_iR_S(D)_{:,f(i)}.                                        \tag{15}
\]
The intervention-pushforward lemma, (14), and (15) now give, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^S\),
\[
\mathcal L\bigl(R_S(C)\varepsilon+T_S(C)x\bigr)
=\mathcal L\bigl(R_S(D)\eta+T_S(D)x\bigr).
\]
The same \(D\) and the same \(\eta\) work for all \(S\), so the full tuple belongs to \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H)\).  This proves
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G)\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H).
\]
Applying the directed equivalence in both orders proves the equality criterion.  No step removes zero columns or replaces a nonvanishing condition by a generic one, so the proof covers the listed cancellation, nullification, invisible-source, source-symmetry, and lower-dimensional strata.

Assume \(\ell=0\).  Then \(C=Q^{-1}\) is square and invertible.  The observational law is the square mixture \(X=C\varepsilon\) of mutually independent nonconstant non-Gaussian sources.  The cited square-ICA uniqueness theorem therefore determines the unordered projective columns of \(C\), equivalently the unordered projective rows
\[
\mathscr R(Q)=\{[Q_{r,:}]:r\in X\}.
\]
Invertibility makes these row classes distinct.  Their zero patterns determine \(\mathbb G_b(\mathscr R(Q))\), and the definition of a perfect matching then determines \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathscr R(Q))\).

Fix \(i\in A\) and write \(U=X\setminus\{i\}\).  Regime solvability gives \(Q_{U,U}^{-1}\).  The intervention-pushforward calculation specializes to
\[
K_{\{i\}}(x)=\mathcal L\bigl(Q_{U,U}^{-1}\varepsilon_U+T_i x\bigr),
\quad T_i=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i}.                                        \tag{22}
\]
Centering gives \(T_i=\partial_x\mathbb E[K_{\{i\}}(x)]\).  At \(x=0\), (22) is a square invertible mixture of the \(n-1\) unaffected independent non-Gaussian sources.  Square-ICA uniqueness identifies the projective rows of its unmixing matrix \(Q_{U,U}\).  If \(v=Q_{r,U}\), \(r\in U\), then (22) gives
\[
vT_i=Q_{r,U}(-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i})=-Q_{r,i}.
\]
Consequently the lift satisfies
\[
\Lambda_i(v,T_i)_U=Q_{r,U},\quad
\Lambda_i(v,T_i)_i=-vT_i=Q_{r,i},
\]
so the lifted residual row classes are exactly \(\{[Q_{r,:}]:r\neq i\}\).  Their unique complement in the observational orbit is \([Q_{i,:}]\).  Looplessness and the normalization \(Q=I_n-B\) give \(Q_{ii}=1\); normalizing the recovered class at coordinate \(i\) therefore yields
\[
e_i^\top-Q_{i,:}=\operatorname{row}_i(B).
\]
This proves the stated row-recovery map, including \(n=2\).

It remains to identify the matching sets.  Any observational matching \(\mu\) normalizes a row-scaled permutation of \(Q\), so for some permutation matrix \(P\) and nonsingular diagonal \(\Delta\),
\[
Q^\mu=\Delta P Q,\quad \varepsilon^\mu=\Delta P\varepsilon,             \tag{23}
\]
and (23) reproduces the observational law with independent legal sources.  If \(\mu([Q_{i,:}])=i\), then \(P\) fixes that row and restricts to a permutation \(P_U\) on \(U\).  Thus
\[
Q^\mu_{U,U}=\Delta_U P_UQ_{U,U},\quad
Q^\mu_{U,i}=\Delta_UP_UQ_{U,i},\quad
\varepsilon^\mu_U=\Delta_UP_U\varepsilon_U.
\]
The response and residual terms in (22) are unchanged:
\[
-(Q^\mu_{U,U})^{-1}Q^\mu_{U,i}=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i},
\quad
(Q^\mu_{U,U})^{-1}\varepsilon^\mu_U=Q_{U,U}^{-1}\varepsilon_U.          \tag{24}
\]
For a matching satisfying the row constraint for every \(i\in A\), the single global representation (23) obeys (24) for every required intervention, so it belongs to \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)\).

Conversely, if a matched mechanism generates the observational and \(i\)-th atomic kernels, the recovery just proved, applied to that common tuple, says that its row assigned label \(i\) must be the unique complement \([Q_{i,:}]\).  Hence every kernel-compatible matching lies in \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{row}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)\).  Together with (23)--(24), this proves
\[
\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)
=\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{row}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)
=\{\mu\in\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathscr R(Q)):
\mu([Q_{i,:}])=i\ \text{for every }i\in A\}.
\]
When \(A=\varnothing\) there is no added row constraint.  When \(A=X\), every row class is fixed at its true label, so only the true matching remains and every row of \(B\) is recovered.

theorem.statement:
Let \(q=|\mathcal I|\), let \(p=nN\), and let \(\lambda\geq1\) be the rational bit length of the labeled graph and intervention input.  There is a terminating exact compiler for both directed cover relations.  It first produces the finite pivot-chart formulas for \(\mathcal D_G\) and \(\mathcal D_H\), then enumerates visible-source subsets and surjections, clears only the nonzero pivot and intervention determinants in the proportionality and simultaneous-response equations, and applies effective sign-condition block elimination to the resulting \(\forall C\,\exists(D,a)\) sentence.  With
\[
s=(q+N+1)2^{8N^2},\quad d=4N^3,\quad \tau=(\lambda+1)2^{8N^2},
\]
and with the absolute effective constant \(c_{\mathrm{qe}}\) of the cited elimination theorem, one directed decision, including a finite sign-cell certificate, uses at most
\[
\mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)
=(\tau+1)^2(s+1)^{(p+1)(p+N+1)+1}
(d+1)^{c_{\mathrm{qe}}(p+1)(p+N+1)}                                   \tag{16}
\]
bit operations.  Hence comparison uses at most \(2\mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)\) bit operations.  Exhaustive enumeration of the equivalence class modulo latent relabeling terminates within
\[
2^{N(N-1)}\bigl(2\mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)+\ell!\,N^2\bigr)               \tag{17}
\]
bit operations, apart from a fixed linear-time encoding overhead.  The certificates and bounds cover forced zeros, punctured fibers, Hall--Rado failures, nullification, and all lower-dimensional incidences; the compiler contains no structural-coefficient or source-law quantifier.
theorem.proof_tex:
We give the compiler and verify each bound.  A rank equality for a matrix with at most \(N\) rows and columns is a finite disjunction over its possible rank, each disjunct asserting that one pivot minor is nonzero and all larger minors vanish.  Apply this to every local system in the definition of \(\mathcal D_G\).  On a selected pivot minor, Gaussian elimination writes an affine base point and a basis of the direction space of \(\mathcal A_j(C)\) as rational functions of \(C\); their denominators are precisely the selected nonzero minors.  Adjoining the base point gives a rational basis of \(W_j(C)\).  Every Hall--Rado condition is then the finite disjunction of nonvanishing minors expressing
\[
\operatorname{rank}[W_j(C):j\in J]\geq |J|,\quad J\subseteq L.
\]
Multiplication by the chart denominators turns it into a Boolean combination of integral polynomial sign conditions without changing its truth on the chart.  The punctured-coordinate tests and the intervention determinants are already rank or nonvanishing conditions.  Thus the exact-realization theorem proves that the resulting quantifier-free formula \(\operatorname{Dom}_G(C)\) defines exactly \(\mathcal D_G\), including its singular and lower-dimensional chart intersections.

For every pair \(U,W\subseteq V\) and every surjection \(f:U\twoheadrightarrow W\), introduce at most \(N\) scalar variables \(a_i\).  The source chart asserts
\[
\begin{aligned}
&C_{:,i}=0\Longleftrightarrow i\notin U,
&&D_{:,j}=0\Longleftrightarrow j\notin W,\\
&a_i\neq0,
&&C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\quad(i\in U).
\end{aligned}                                                           \tag{18}
\]
Column nonzeroness is the polynomial inequality \(\sum_{r\in X}C_{ri}^2>0\).  On the domain charts, simultaneous response equality is polynomialized without introducing an inverse:
\[
C_{O,S}\operatorname{adj}(C_{S,S})\det(D_{S,S})
=D_{O,S}\operatorname{adj}(D_{S,S})\det(C_{S,S}),
\quad O=X\setminus S.                                                    \tag{19}
\]
The domain formulas guarantee that both multiplied determinants are nonzero, so (19) is equivalent to \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\).

Let \(\Theta_f(C,D,a)\) be the conjunction of \(\operatorname{Dom}_H(D)\), (18), and (19) for every \(S\in\mathcal I\).  The compiler decides the explicit sentence
\[
\Phi_{G,H}:\quad
\forall C\in\mathbb R^{n\times N}\;
\left[\operatorname{Dom}_G(C)\Longrightarrow
\bigvee_{U,W,f}\exists D\in\mathbb R^{n\times N}\exists a\in\mathbb R^{U}\;
\Theta_f(C,D,a)\right].                                                  \tag{20}
\]
By the definition of directed cover and the exact mixing and source-partition theorems, (20) is true exactly when \(\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\) holds.  Thus (20) has eliminated both the matrix \(B\) and all source distributions before real-algebraic elimination is invoked; it is not the original feasibility question.

We now justify the advertised finite input bounds.  Each local or pivot matrix has at most \(N\) rows and columns and therefore at most \(2^{2N}\) minors.  Choosing pivot data for at most \(N\) local systems gives at most \(2^{2N^2}\) joint charts.  A concatenated Hall matrix has at most \(N\) rows and \(N^2\) columns, hence fewer than \(2^{N+N^2}\) minors.  The \(2^\ell\) Hall subfamilies, all their rank minors, the \(q\) intervention blocks, and the Boolean zero-pattern formulas multiply the chart count by less than \((q+N+1)2^{4N^2}\).  Finally, the number of pairs of visible subsets and partial source maps is at most \(2^{2N}(N+1)^N\leq2^{3N^2}\) for \(N\geq2\).  Sharing repeated atoms in the Boolean formula gives the conservative bound \(s=(q+N+1)2^{8N^2}\).  Pivot numerators and denominators are minors of degree at most \(N\); a Hall minor contains at most \(N\) such entries, and clearing at most \(N\) chart denominators has degree below \(4N^3\).  Equations (18)--(19) have smaller degree.  Expanding determinants and cleared products by the Leibniz rule, at every one of fewer than \(2^{8N^2}\) recorded atoms, gives coefficient bit length at most \(\tau=(\lambda+1)2^{8N^2}\).  These deliberately loose inequalities also cover empty blocks.

Sentence (20) has two quantifier blocks of sizes at most \(p\) and \(p+N\).  The cited effective block-elimination theorem, followed by exact integer arithmetic with its stated intermediate bit-length bound, therefore gives exactly (16) after fixing its one absolute constant \(c_{\mathrm{qe}}\).  Its output sign conditions, Thom encodings of sample points, and truth labels form a finite checkable certificate.  Sign decomposition explicitly retains zero signs, so forced-zero, nullification, and lower-dimensional cells are not discarded.  Run this procedure in both directions and use the coupled-equivalence theorem to decide equality.

There are exactly \(2^{N(N-1)}\) labeled loopless digraphs.  Test each against \(G\).  To quotient only latent relabeling, compute the lexicographically least adjacency encoding among the \(\ell!\) simultaneous row-and-column permutations fixing every observed label; each comparison costs at most \(N^2\) bit operations.  This proves (17), termination, and completeness of the enumerated class.

There is an absolute effective constant \(c_{\mathrm{qe}}\) with the following property.  A first-order formula over a real closed field, built from \(s\) polynomials of degree at most \(d\), with quantifier-block sizes \(k_1,\ldots,k_\omega\), admits effective block elimination.  The arithmetic-operation count and the degrees and integer coefficient bit lengths of the output are bounded by the block-elimination bounds in Theorem 2.27 of the cited source; in particular, for two blocks and no free variables, a bit-operation bound of the form
\[
(\tau+1)^2(s+1)^{(k_1+1)(k_2+1)+1}(d+1)^{c_{\mathrm{qe}}(k_1+1)(k_2+1)}
\]
is valid after increasing \(c_{\mathrm{qe}}\) once and using ordinary exact integer arithmetic.  The output includes the finite sign conditions and algebraic sample descriptions needed to verify the truth value.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(k,p,q\) be nonnegative integers and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times p}\) and \(D\in\mathbb R^{k\times q}\).  Write \(U_A\) and \(U_D\) for their sets of nonzero columns, and let \(\mathscr L(A)\) be the set of laws of \(A\xi\) as the coordinates of \(\xi\) range independently over all centered, nonconstant, non-Gaussian real laws with finite second moments.  Then \(\mathscr L(A)\subseteq\mathscr L(D)\) if and only if there are a surjection \(f:U_A\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero real numbers \(a_i\), \(i\in U_A\), such that \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\) for every \(i\in U_A\).  This includes \(k=0\) and zero columns.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(r=|U_A|\).  If \(r=0\), then \(A\xi=0\) almost surely.  Containment is possible precisely when \(U_D=\varnothing\), and the unique empty map is the required surjection.  Hence suppose \(r>0\).

We first prove necessity.  Let \(F\) be the subfield of \(\mathbb R\) generated by all entries of \(A\).  It is countable.  Choose positive numbers \((r_i)_{i\in U_A}\) algebraically independent over \(F\), and set \(h_i=r_iA_{:,i}\).  If \(\sum_i m_i h_i=0\) with \(m_i\in\mathbb Z\), then each coordinate gives a polynomial relation \(\sum_i m_iA_{vi}r_i=0\) over \(F\).  Algebraic independence makes every coefficient \(m_iA_{vi}\) zero; because column \(i\) is nonzero, \(m_i=0\).  Thus
\[
\Lambda:=\bigoplus_{i\in U_A}\mathbb Z h_i
\]
is a free abelian group on the displayed generators.

Fix \(p_i\in(0,1)\), let \(Z_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)\) independently, and take \(\xi_i=r_i(Z_i-p_i)\) for \(i\in U_A\); choose independent centered two-point laws for the zero columns.  Every source is centered, nonconstant, non-Gaussian, and has finite variance.  The law of \(A\xi\) has the \(2^r\) distinct support points
\[
-\sum_i p_i h_i+\sum_i z_i h_i,\quad z_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
By the assumed containment it also equals the law of \(\sum_{j\in U_D}Y_j\), where \(Y_j=D_{:,j}\eta_j\) and the \(\eta_j\)'s are independent legal sources.  The topological support of a convolution of finitely many probability measures contains the Minkowski sum of their supports: neighborhoods of chosen support points have positive probability, and independence gives positive probability to their sum.  Since the support of the sum is finite, fixing one support point of every other summand shows that each \(Y_j\) has finite support.  It is therefore purely atomic, and every point in its support has positive mass.

Choose \(y_j^0\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\).  If \(y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), the two sums obtained by using respectively \(y\) and \(y_j^0\), while holding the other support points fixed, belong to the original cube support.  Their difference is in \(\Lambda\).  Freeness of \(\Lambda\) gives a unique exponent vector \(\nu_j(y)\in\mathbb Z^{U_A}\) satisfying \(y-y_j^0=\sum_i\nu_j(y)_i h_i\).  Hence the probability generating Laurent polynomial
\[
F_j(z):=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)}\Pr(Y_j=y)z^{\nu_j(y)}
\]
is defined in \(\mathbb R[z_i^{\pm1}:i\in U_A]\).  Independence and equality of the two laws imply
\[
\prod_{j\in U_D}F_j(z)
=c z^\gamma\prod_{i\in U_A}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\bigr)                 \tag{1}
\]
for a positive constant \(c\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb Z^{U_A}\); equality holds coefficient by coefficient because the map from exponent vectors to \(\Lambda\) is injective.

For completeness, the algebra used in (1) is elementary.  Gauss's primitive-polynomial argument, applied inductively, makes \(\mathbb R[z_i:i\in U_A]\) a unique-factorization domain, and localizing at the monomials preserves unique factorization.  Each factor \((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\) is primitive and linear in \(z_i\), hence prime, and factors belonging to distinct variables are nonassociated.  Unique factorization in (1) therefore yields a partition \((I_j)_{j\in U_D}\) of \(U_A\) such that, up to a positive constant and a Laurent monomial,
\[
F_j(z)=c_jz^{\gamma_j}\prod_{i\in I_j}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\bigr).       \tag{2}
\]
Because \(D_{:,j}\neq0\) and \(\eta_j\) is nonconstant, \(Y_j\) is nonconstant, so \(I_j\neq\varnothing\).  If \(i\in I_j\), two monomials on the right of (2), obtained by changing only the \(i\)-th Bernoulli choice, show that \(h_i\) is a difference of two support points of \(Y_j\).  Those points lie on the line \(\mathbb RD_{:,j}\), whence \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,j}\) for a nonzero \(a_i\).  Defining \(f(i)=j\) for \(i\in I_j\) gives the asserted surjection.

Conversely, suppose such \(f\) and \((a_i)\) are given.  For \(j\in U_D\) define
\[
\eta_j=\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\xi_i.
\]
The fibers of \(f\) are disjoint and nonempty, so these variables are mutually independent and centered.  Their variances are
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\eta_j)=\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(\xi_i)>0,
\]
which proves nonconstancy and finite second moments.  The cited L\'evy--Cram\'er theorem, applied inductively, shows that \(\eta_j\) cannot be Gaussian, since otherwise every nonconstant summand \(a_i\xi_i\) would be Gaussian.  Give every \(j\notin U_D\) an arbitrary independent centered two-point source.  The resulting source vector is legal and
\[
D\eta=\sum_{j\in U_D}D_{:,j}\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\xi_i
=\sum_{i\in U_A}A_{:,i}\xi_i=A\xi.
\]
This proves sufficiency and the lemma.

For a direction \(G\to H\), a source matrix \(C\in\mathcal D_G\), and \(S\in\mathcal I\), let \(\mathcal W_S(C)\) be the finite union, over visible-column subsets and source surjections, of all triples \((D,f_S,a_S)\) with \(D\in\mathcal D_H\), \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\), and
\[
R_S(C)_{:,i}=(a_S)_iR_S(D)_{:,f_S(i)}
\]
for every visible column of \(R_S(C)\).  Let \(\mathcal W_\star(C)\) be the observational witness set consisting of triples \((D,f,a)\) with \(C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\).  Then regime-wise projected containment holds exactly when \(\mathcal W_S(C)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(C\in\mathcal D_G\), while joint containment holds exactly when every \(C\in\mathcal D_G\) has a rooted witness \((D,f,a)\in\mathcal W_\star(C)\) satisfying \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\) simultaneously for all \(S\in\mathcal I\).  For such a rooted witness its one observational source partition induces every residual partition, so the transition graph has a global section precisely when all regime vertices attach to one root; all transition compositions then agree automatically.  Consequently, equality of all single-regime projections implies joint equality for the pair \((G,H)\) if and only if this rooted common-lift condition holds in both directions whenever all the individual \(\mathcal W_S(C)\)'s are nonempty.  This condition is a finite semialgebraic test decided by the effective population compiler.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For a fixed \(S\), the intervention-pushforward lemma writes the kernel as an affine translate with slope \(T_S(C)\) and residual mixing matrix \(R_S(C)\).  Equality of centered kernel means forces equality of slopes.  Apply the finite-mixture containment lemma to the two residual matrices; it gives exactly the source-surjection and proportionality clauses defining \(\mathcal W_S(C)\).  Quantifying over \(C\in\mathcal D_G\) proves the regime-wise assertion.

Because \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), \(R_\varnothing(C)=C\) and \(T_\varnothing\) is empty.  Thus any joint witness must begin at a member of \(\mathcal W_\star(C)=\mathcal W_\varnothing(C)\).  If \((D,f,a)\) is such a root and all response matrices agree, then for every \(S\) and every \(i\in U_C\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_S(C)_{:,i}
&=C_{X\setminus S,i}-T_S(C)C_{S,i}\\
&=a_i\bigl(D_{X\setminus S,f(i)}-T_S(D)D_{S,f(i)}\bigr)
=a_iR_S(D)_{:,f(i)}.
\end{aligned}                                                           \tag{21}
\]
Columns made zero by (21) are simply omitted from the residual visible sets; several fibers may merge further, which is allowed by the finite-mixture lemma.  Hence one root induces compatible witnesses at all regime vertices.  Conversely, a global common mechanism has one observed mixing matrix \(D\), and its observational equality supplies one root partition; equality of every affine mean supplies all the simultaneous response equations.  It therefore yields exactly such a rooted section.  This proves necessity and sufficiency.

Every set in the construction is a finite union of the same pivot, zero-pattern, surjection, and response sign charts used in (18)--(20).  A transition edge merely repeats equality of the common \(D\)-coordinates and the induced proportionalities (21).  Thus existence of a rooted section is a finite first-order sign condition and is decided by the established compiler.  Applying the argument to both directions proves the final equivalence characterization.  Notice that nonempty regime fibers alone need not select the same root; the proof does not assert that such a selection always exists for graph-generated fibers.

proofs.proof_tex:
By Definition \texttt{def:witness-mechanisms}, an arbitrary admissible mechanism on \(G_\star\) can be written
\[
 L=\varepsilon_L,\quad
 X_1=cL+aX_2+\varepsilon_1,\quad
 X_2=bX_1+\varepsilon_2,\quad
 X_3=dL+\varepsilon_3,
\]
where \(a,b,c,d\ne0\) and \(1-ab\ne0\).  By Definition \texttt{def:exact-support-model-class}, as incorporated in Definition \texttt{def:graph-law-set}, the sources are mutually independent, centered, nonconstant, non-Gaussian, and have finite second moments.  Define
\[
 \alpha=b^{-1},\quad \beta=a^{-1},\quad
 \gamma=-ca^{-1},\quad \delta=d
\]
and define new sources by
\[
 \eta_L=\varepsilon_L,\quad
 \eta_1=-b^{-1}\varepsilon_2,\quad
 \eta_2=-a^{-1}\varepsilon_1,\quad
 \eta_3=\varepsilon_3.
\]
Every displayed division is licensed by \(ab\ne0\).  A permutation of mutually independent random variables followed by nonzero coordinatewise rescaling preserves mutual independence and centering.  It also preserves nonconstancy and non-Gaussianity: if \(rY\) were constant or Gaussian for \(r\ne0\), then \(Y=r^{-1}(rY)\) would have the same forbidden property.  Finally,
\[
 \mathbb E[\eta_1^2]=b^{-2}\mathbb E[\varepsilon_2^2],
 \quad
 \mathbb E[\eta_2^2]=a^{-2}\mathbb E[\varepsilon_1^2],
\]
and the other two second moments are unchanged, so the transformed sources still have finite second moments.

The resulting \(H_\star\) equations are satisfied by the same endogenous vector, sample by sample.  Indeed, using respectively the \(G_\star\) equations for \(X_2\) and \(X_1\),
\[
 \alpha X_2+\eta_1
 =b^{-1}(X_2-\varepsilon_2)
 =X_1,
\]
and
\[
 \gamma L+\beta X_1+\eta_2
 =-ca^{-1}L+a^{-1}(X_1-\varepsilon_1)
 =X_2.
\]
Also \(L=\eta_L\) and \(X_3=\delta L+\eta_3\).  Thus the observed vectors coincide almost surely under this coupling and consequently have the same law.

The transformation remains inside the exact-support parameter space.  Its four structural coefficients are nonzero because \(a,b,c,d\ne0\), and the two feedback determinants obey
\[
 1-\alpha\beta
 =1-\frac1{ab}
 =\frac{ab-1}{ab}\ne0.
\]
More explicitly, in the order \((L,X_1,X_2,X_3)\), the only directed cycle in either graph is the \(X_1,X_2\) two-cycle.  Hence for any observed intervention target \(S\), the principal structural determinant is \(1-ab\) for \(G_\star\), respectively \(1-\alpha\beta\) for \(H_\star\), when \(S\cap\{X_1,X_2\}=\varnothing\), and it is \(1\) when \(S\cap\{X_1,X_2\}\ne\varnothing\).  Thus the invertibility required by Assumption \texttt{ass:regime-solvability} holds in every regime; in particular, no stability condition has been used.

Conversely, take arbitrary nonzero \(H_\star\) coefficients \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) with \(1-\alpha\beta\ne0\) and admissible sources \(\eta\).  Set
\[
 a=\beta^{-1},\quad b=\alpha^{-1},\quad
 c=-\gamma\beta^{-1},\quad d=\delta,
\]
and
\[
 \varepsilon_L=\eta_L,\quad
 \varepsilon_1=-\beta^{-1}\eta_2,\quad
 \varepsilon_2=-\alpha^{-1}\eta_1,\quad
 \varepsilon_3=\eta_3.
\]
The same preservation argument makes this an admissible \(G_\star\) source tuple, while
\[
 1-ab=1-\frac1{\alpha\beta}
 =\frac{\alpha\beta-1}{\alpha\beta}\ne0.
\]
Direct substitution shows that this is the inverse of the preceding transformation on both coefficients and source laws.  Therefore it is a bijection between the entire exact-support observational parameter spaces, and its coupled endogenous solutions agree.  By Definition \texttt{def:graph-law-set},
\[
 \mathcal P_{\{\varnothing\}}(G_\star)
 =\mathcal P_{\{\varnothing\}}(H_\star).
\]

It remains to show that the singleton intervention distinguishes the graphs.  By Assumption \texttt{ass:perfect-intervention}, intervention at \(X_1=z\) deletes the equation for \(X_1\) and leaves all other equations and unaffected source laws unchanged.  For an arbitrary \(G_\star\) mechanism this gives
\[
 L=\varepsilon_L,\quad
 X_2=bz+\varepsilon_2,\quad
 X_3=d\varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_3.
\]
All covariances below exist by Assumption \texttt{ass:source-second-moment}.  Assumption \texttt{ass:source-independence} therefore yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)
 &=d\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_L)
   +\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3)\\
 &=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]

For an arbitrary \(H_\star\) mechanism, write its equations as
\[
 L=\eta_L,\quad
 X_1=\alpha X_2+\eta_1,\quad
 X_2=\gamma L+\beta X_1+\eta_2,\quad
 X_3=\delta L+\eta_3.
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:exact-support} gives \(\gamma\delta\ne0\).  Under the same intervention,
\[
 X_2=\gamma\eta_L+\beta z+\eta_2,
 \quad
 X_3=\delta\eta_L+\eta_3.
\]
Expanding covariance and using Assumption \texttt{ass:source-independence} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)
 &=\gamma\delta\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L)
   +\gamma\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_L,\eta_3)
   +\delta\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_2,\eta_L)
   +\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_2,\eta_3)\\
 &=\gamma\delta\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:source-nondegeneracy}, together with the finite second moment, implies \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L)>0\), so this covariance is nonzero.  Under the inverse parametrization above, \(\gamma=-c/a\), \(\delta=d\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L)=\sigma_L^2\); hence
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)
 =-\frac ca d\sigma_L^2\ne0.
\]

Covariance is determined by a probability law having finite second moments.  Thus no \(G_\star\) singleton-intervention kernel can equal an \(H_\star\) singleton-intervention kernel.  If \(\{X_1\}\in\mathcal I\), equality of two joint response-kernel tuples would imply equality of those singleton components, which is impossible.  Both model sets are nonempty, for example with any allowed coefficients and mutually independent centered Laplace sources.  Consequently
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G_\star)
 \ne
 \mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H_\star)
 \quad\text{whenever }\{X_1\}\in\mathcal I.
\]
No treatment-overlap or positivity premise is relevant because the objects compared are population perfect-intervention kernels indexed by fixed \(z\); no boundary or limiting argument is used.

Under \(\operatorname{do}(X_1=z)\), every \(G_\star\) kernel satisfies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)=0\), whereas every \(H_\star\) kernel satisfies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)=-(c/a)d\sigma_L^2\ne0\). Fix \(G\in\mathcal F\), and write \(e(G)=|E(G)|\).  Define a coefficient matrix \(B^{G}\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\) by
\[
 B^{G}_{ji}=\begin{cases}
 \beta,& i\to j\text{ is an edge of }G,\\
 0,& i\to j\text{ is not an edge of }G.
 \end{cases}
\]
Because \(G\) is loopless, \(B^{G}_{ii}=0\) for every \(i\in V\).  By the definition of \(B^{G}\),
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(B^{G})=E(G)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 |B^{G}_{ji}|=\beta\quad\text{for every }i\to j\text{ in }G.
\]
Thus the exact-support and edge-margin clauses in \(\mathfrak K_G(L_B,\kappa,\beta,s_-,s_+)\) hold.

There are at most \(N(N-1)\) directed edges in a loopless digraph on \(N\) labeled vertices.  The operator norm is bounded by the Frobenius norm, so
\[
 \lVert B^{G}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \lVert B^{G}\rVert_{F}
 =\beta\sqrt{e(G)}
 \le\beta\sqrt{N(N-1)}
 \le N\beta
 \le\frac18.
\]
The last inequality uses \(0<\beta\le 1/(8N)\).  Since \(L_B\ge1\), this also gives \(\lVert B^{G}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_B\), as required by the coefficient-bound clause.

Fix \(S\in\mathcal I\) and put \(R=V\setminus S\).  The principal submatrix \(B^{G}_{R,R}\) is a coordinate compression of \(B^{G}\), whence
\[
 \lVert B^{G}_{R,R}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \lVert B^{G}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le\frac18.
\]
For every \(y\in\mathbb R^{R}\), the reverse triangle inequality therefore yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lVert Q_{R,R}y\rVert_2
 &=\lVert (I_R-B^{G}_{R,R})y\rVert_2\\
 &\ge \lVert y\rVert_2-\lVert B^{G}_{R,R}y\rVert_2\\
 &\ge \bigl(1-\lVert B^{G}_{R,R}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\bigr)\lVert y\rVert_2\\
 &\ge\frac78\lVert y\rVert_2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\lVert y\rVert_2=1\) gives
\[
 \sigma_{\min}(Q_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S})\ge\frac78\ge\kappa,
\]
where the final inequality uses \(0<\kappa\le1/2\).  If \(R=\varnothing\), the displayed lower-bound formulation is vacuous and the unique linear map on the zero-dimensional space is invertible; equivalently, the minimum-singular-value margin is satisfied under the standard zero-dimensional convention.  Hence the inverse-margin clause holds for every \(S\in\mathcal I\), and in particular every required structural subsystem is invertible.

Choose any \(s^{\circ}\in(s_-,s_+)\), for example \(s^{\circ}=(s_-+s_+)/2\), and set \(s_i=s^{\circ}\) for every \(i\in V\).  On a finite product probability space, let \((Z_i)_{i\in V}\) be independent variables having density \(z\mapsto e^{-|z|}/2\), and define \(\varepsilon_i=s_iZ_i\).  Then each \(s_i\in[s_-,s_+]\), so the Laplace-scale clause holds.  Moreover, direct integration gives
\[
 \mathbb E|Z_i|^4
 =\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|z|^4e^{-|z|}\,dz
 =\int_0^{\infty}z^4e^{-z}\,dz
 =4!
 =24.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathbb E|\varepsilon_i|^4
 =s_i^4\mathbb E|Z_i|^4
 =24s_i^4
 \le24s_+^4
 \qquad(i\in V).
\]
All clauses in the definition of \(\mathfrak K_G(L_B,\kappa,\beta,s_-,s_+)\) are therefore satisfied by \((B^{G},(s_i)_{i\in V})\).  Since \(G\in\mathcal F\) was arbitrary, the compact Laplace class is nonempty for every \(G\in\mathcal F\), with the claimed uniform fourth-moment bound.

Fix a graph \(G\in\mathcal F\), and let \(e_G=|E(G)|\).  Write
\(\theta=(B,s)\), where \(s=(s_i)_{i\in V}\), and let
\(\Theta_G\subseteq\mathbb R^{e_G+N}\) be the parameter set in
\(\mathfrak K_G(L_B,\kappa,\beta,s_-,s_+)\), with the off-graph entries of
\(B\) suppressed from the coordinates.  The exact-support and edge-margin
conditions say, separately for each edge coordinate,
\[
 B_{ji}\in[-L_B,-\beta]\cup[\beta,L_B].
\]
The upper bound follows from
\(|B_{ji}|=|e_j^{\mathsf T}Be_i|\leq\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_B\).
The scale coordinates lie in \([s_-,s_+]\).  Each of these coordinate
conditions is closed.  The maps \(B\mapsto\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\)
and
\(B\mapsto\sigma_{\min}(I-B_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S})\) are continuous.
Consequently \(\Theta_G\) is a closed and bounded subset of the
finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^{e_G+N}\), hence is compact.  Notice
that the lower edge margin is essential here: exact nonzero support without
that margin would not be a closed condition.

We first derive the response law and the continuity bounds used by the
certifier.  Fix \(S\in\mathcal I\), put \(W=V\setminus S\) and
\(O=X\setminus S\), and let \(P_O\) and \(P_W\) denote coordinate
projections.  Under the surgical intervention \(\operatorname{do}(X_S=x)\),
the nonintervened equations are
\[
 (I-B_{W,W})V_W=B_{W,S}x+\varepsilon_W.
\]
The inverse-margin assumption gives
\[
 \bigl\|(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq \kappa^{-1},
\]
so the retained random output is
\[
 Y_{S,x}=A_S(B)x+H_S(B)\operatorname{diag}(s)Z,
 \qquad
 A_S(B)=P_O(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}B_{W,S},
\]
\[
 H_S(B)=P_O(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}P_W^{\mathsf T}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Here columns of \(H_S(B)\) indexed by \(S\) are zero.  This equation uses
only surgical intervention and the displayed inverse margin; it neither
removes nor separates any latent source.

For completeness, (1) agrees with the maps in the certified construction.
Let \(Q=I-B\), \(K=Q^{-1}\), and order the coordinates as \((S,W)\).
The empty intervention belongs to \(\mathcal I\), so the inverse-margin
condition at \(S=\varnothing\) makes \(Q\) invertible.  Since \(Q_{W,W}\)
is also invertible, block elimination gives that \(K_{S,S}\) is invertible
and
\[
 K_{W,S}K_{S,S}^{-1}
   =-Q_{W,W}^{-1}Q_{W,S}
   =Q_{W,W}^{-1}B_{W,S},
 \tag{2}
\]
as well as
\[
 K_{W,:}-K_{W,S}K_{S,S}^{-1}K_{S,:}
   =\bigl[0,\,Q_{W,W}^{-1}\bigr].
 \tag{3}
\]
Restricting (2)--(3) to the rows \(O\), and using
\(C=K_{X,:}\), proves
\[
 A_S(B)=T_S(C),\qquad H_S(B)=R_S(C).
 \tag{4}
\]
The identities have their usual empty-matrix interpretation when
\(S=\varnothing\); settings with \(O=\varnothing\) are not retained.

For a standard centered Laplace variable, direct integration of its density
gives
\[
 \mathbb E\exp(iuZ_i)
 =\int_0^\infty e^{-z}\cos(uz)\,dz
 =(1+u^2)^{-1}.
\]
Independence of the \(Z_i\)'s and (1)--(4) therefore yield, for every retained
setting \(v=(S,x)\),
\[
 \phi_{G,\theta,v}(t)
 =\exp\!\bigl(i t^{\mathsf T}T_S(C)x\bigr)
   \prod_{i\in V}
   \left(1+s_i^2[R_S(C)^{\mathsf T}t]_i^2\right)^{-1}.
 \tag{5}
\]
Thus (5) is the characteristic function of the causal response law, rather
than a definition of that law.

We next give explicit uniform moduli.  For two feasible parameters
\(\theta=(B,s)\) and \(\theta'=(B',s')\), the resolvent identity gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 &(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}-(I-B'_{W,W})^{-1}\\
 &\quad=(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}(B_{W,W}-B'_{W,W})
          (I-B'_{W,W})^{-1}.
 \end{split}
\]
Hence
\[
 \lVert H_S(B)-H_S(B')\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\kappa^{-2}\lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Adding and subtracting
\(P_O(I-B_{W,W})^{-1}B'_{W,S}\), and using
\(\lVert B'_{W,S}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_B\), similarly gives
\[
 \lVert A_S(B)-A_S(B')\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq(\kappa^{-1}+L_B\kappa^{-2})
       \lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.
 \tag{7}
\]
These are precisely the required inverse-resolvent and response moduli.

Couple the two laws by using the same vector \(Z\).  Since a standard
Laplace variable has second moment \(2\), Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \mathbb E\lVert Z\rVert_2
 \leq\bigl(\mathbb E\lVert Z\rVert_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}
 =\sqrt{2N}.
\]
All retained intervention values are zero or a coordinate unit vector, and
therefore satisfy \(\lVert x\rVert_2\leq1\).  From (6)--(7),
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathbb E\lVert Y_{S,x}(\theta)-Y_{S,x}(\theta')\rVert_2
 \leq{}&c_B\lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
       +c_s\lVert s-s'\rVert_\infty,\\
 c_B={}&\kappa^{-1}+L_B\kappa^{-2}
          +\sqrt{2N}s_+\kappa^{-2},\\
 c_s={}&\sqrt{2N}\kappa^{-1}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, the three terms in \(c_B\) respectively bound the two terms in
(7) and the change of the residual mixing matrix in (6), while \(c_s\)
bounds the scale change using
\(\lVert H_S(B')\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa^{-1}\).
The elementary inequality \(|e^{iu}-e^{iv}|\leq|u-v|\) then implies
\[
 |\phi_{G,\theta,v}(t)-\phi_{G,\theta',v}(t)|
 \leq\lVert t\rVert_2
 \left(c_B\lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
       +c_s\lVert s-s'\rVert_\infty\right).
 \tag{9}
\]

Equation (5) also proves continuity of the parameter-to-law map in the
metric \(d\).  Explicitly, for any integer \(J\), the first \(J\) terms in
\(d\) are continuous by (5), while the remaining terms are uniformly bounded
by
\[
 \frac1M\sum_{v=1}^M\sum_{j>J}2^{-j}\,2=2^{1-J}.
 \tag{10}
\]
First choosing \(J\) to make (10) small and then applying finite-term
continuity proves continuity in \(d\).  The image \(K_G\) of the compact set
\(\Theta_G\) is consequently compact.  Since \(\mathcal F\) is finite, this
holds simultaneously for every candidate graph.

We now make the certified optimization and its termination explicit.  Given
the data, define
\[
 \widehat\phi_{v,j}
 =\frac1m\sum_{r=1}^m
   \exp\!\left(i t_{k_v,j}^{\mathsf T}Y_{v,r}\right)
\]
and, for \(J=J_m\),
\[
 f_{G,m}(\theta)
 =\frac1M\sum_{v=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^{J}2^{-j}
   |\widehat\phi_{v,j}-\phi_{G,\theta,v}(t_{k_v,j})|,
 \qquad
 \widehat D_{G,m}=\min_{\theta\in\Theta_G}f_{G,m}(\theta).
 \tag{11}
\]
The minimum exists by compactness and continuity.  If every free coordinate
of \(\theta-\theta'\) is at most \(h\) in absolute value, then
\(\lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\lVert B-B'\rVert_{\mathrm F}\leq Nh\) and
\(\lVert s-s'\rVert_\infty\leq h\).  The frequency condition and
\(\sum_{j\geq1}j2^{-j}=2\), together with (9), show that
\[
 |f_{G,m}(\theta)-f_{G,m}(\theta')|
 \leq \Lambda h,
 \qquad
 \Lambda=2\sqrt N\,(Nc_B+c_s).
 \tag{12}
\]
This modulus is uniform in \(G\), \(m\), the data, and the retained setting.

Here is a finite certifier that also handles lower-dimensional feasible
faces.  Split the \(e_G\) edge coordinates into their \(2^{e_G}\) sign
boxes.  On each sign box, the constraints defining \(\Theta_G\) are finitely
many rational polynomial weak inequalities: for example,
\[
 L_B^2I-B^{\mathsf T}B\succeq0,
 \qquad
 (I-B_{W,W})^{\mathsf T}(I-B_{W,W})-\kappa^2I\succeq0,
 \tag{13}
\]
where each positive-semidefinite condition is represented by nonnegativity
of all its principal minors.  Coordinate-box inequalities complete this
finite list.  Subdivide every coordinate interval into rational intervals of
width at most \(h\).  Feasibility of each resulting closed box is decided by
a finite sign decomposition of the polynomials in (13): project successively
by adjoining their coefficients, discriminants, and pairwise resultants;
isolate the finitely many univariate roots by signed remainder sequences;
and lift through all root sections and open sectors.  At every projection the
number of variables decreases by one, and every list consists of finitely
many finite-degree polynomials.  The recursion therefore terminates.  Signs
are constant on each lifted sector, while root sections are retained, so a
weak-inequality feasible cell is found if and only if one exists.  In
particular, the procedure does not discard a feasible point merely because
it lies on an edge-margin, norm, or singular-value boundary.

For an explicit finite work bound, put
\[
 q=e_G+N\leq N^2,
 \quad W_0=\max\{L_B,s_+-s_-\},
 \quad r_0=(1+|\mathcal I|)(2^N-1)+2q,
 \quad d_0=2N,
\]
and recursively set
\[
 r_{a+1}=4r_a^2d_a^2,
 \qquad d_{a+1}=2d_a^2
 \quad(0\leq a<q).
 \tag{14}
\]
The displayed projection construction uses no more than the right-hand side
of (14) as a coarse bound on, respectively, its next polynomial count and
degree.  Thus, for tolerance governed by mesh \(h\), at most
\[
 2^{e_G}\left(1+\left\lceil W_0/h\right\rceil\right)^q
 \prod_{a=0}^{q-1}(2r_ad_a+1)
 \tag{15}
\]
lifted grid cells are inspected, and each retained sample requires \(MJ_m\)
evaluations of (5).  This deliberately coarse bound is finite and depends
only on the displayed finite input sizes, rational bounds, and requested
tolerance.

Choose one algebraic sample point in every nonempty grid box, including root
sections.  Formula (5), rational matrix arithmetic, and interval evaluation
of sine and cosine give certified rational enclosures of (11); range reduction
followed by the alternating power series supplies any requested finite
precision.  This is also valid in the usual computable-real representation
of the observed coordinates, relative to their Cauchy names.  If
\(f_b\) denotes the value at the chosen point of a nonempty box \(b\), then
(12) gives
\[
 \min_b f_b-\Lambda h
 \leq \widehat D_{G,m}\leq\min_b f_b.
 \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, every feasible parameter and the chosen feasible point in its grid
box are within coordinate distance \(h\).  Taking a rational
\(h\leq\epsilon_m/(4\Lambda)\) and evaluating the finitely many \(f_b\)'s
with total outward-rounding width at most \(\epsilon_m/2\) produces a
certified interval
\[
 [\underline D_{G,m},\overline D_{G,m}]
 \ni\widehat D_{G,m},
 \qquad
 \eta_{G,m}:=\overline D_{G,m}-\underline D_{G,m}\leq\epsilon_m.
 \tag{17}
\]
If there is no feasible cell, the same finite sign decomposition certifies
\(\Theta_G=\varnothing\); the algorithm assigns discrepancy \(+\infty\) and
excludes \(G\).  All minima in (11), (16), and (17) concern the nonempty case.
Coverage assertions for an empty \(K_G\) are vacuous, and such a graph is
automatically rejected in the separation assertion.
Because \(\epsilon_m>0\) is a computable real, directed approximation produces
in finite time a rational \(r_m\) such that
\(\epsilon_m\leq r_m\leq2\epsilon_m\).  Set
\(\rho_m=r_m-\epsilon_m\), so \(0\leq\rho_m\leq\epsilon_m\).  The two
quantities actually compared, \(\underline D_{G,m}\) and \(r_m\), are
rational; a tie is included.  Hence the procedure terminates and is
measurable.  In the notation of the frozen construction, its certified
tolerance is \(\rho_m\), and it includes \(G\) whenever
\[
 \underline D_{G,m}\leq r_m=\epsilon_m+\rho_m.
 \tag{18}
\]
Equations (12), (15), and (17) prove, rather than assume, the claimed global
optimization certification.

It remains to prove the probability statements.  We first derive the stated
simultaneous radius.  If \(U\in[-1,1]\) and \(\mu=\mathbb EU\), convexity of
the exponential gives
\[
 e^{\lambda u}\leq\frac{1+u}{2}e^\lambda
                     +\frac{1-u}{2}e^{-\lambda}
 \quad(-1\leq u\leq1).
\]
After expectation and multiplication by \(e^{-\lambda\mu}\), the logarithm
of the right-hand side is
\(g(\lambda)=\log(\cosh\lambda+\mu\sinh\lambda)-\lambda\mu\).
It has \(g(0)=g'(0)=0\), and \(g''(\lambda)\) is the variance of a random
variable supported on \(\{-1,1\}\), so \(g''(\lambda)\leq1\).  Twice
integrating this inequality proves
\[
 \mathbb E e^{\lambda(U-\mu)}\leq e^{\lambda^2/2}.
\]
Independence within a retained setting, exponential Markov inequality, and
optimization at \(\lambda=a\) therefore give
\[
 \Pr\left\{\left|m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^mU_r-\mu\right|>a\right\}
 \leq2e^{-ma^2/2}.
 \tag{19}
\]
Both the real and imaginary parts of
\(\exp(i t_{k_v,j}^{\mathsf T}Y_{v,r})\) lie in \([-1,1]\).  If the complex
empirical error exceeds \(a\), one of those two real errors exceeds
\(a/\sqrt2\).  Applying (19) and taking a union bound over the \(MJ_m\)
features yields
\[
 \Pr_P\left\{
   \max_{v\leq M,\,j\leq J_m}
   |\widehat\phi_{v,j}-\phi_{P_v}(t_{k_v,j})|>a
 \right\}
 \leq4MJ_m e^{-ma^2/4}.
 \tag{20}
\]
With
\(a=\epsilon_m=2\sqrt{\log(4MJ_m/\alpha)/m}\), the right-hand side of
(20) is \(\alpha\).  This proves the requested simultaneous
real-and-imaginary radius with its stated constant.

Suppose now that \(P\in K_G\), and choose a generating
\(\theta_0\in\Theta_G\).  On the event complementary to that in (20),
\[
 \begin{split}
 \widehat D_{G,m}
 &\leq f_{G,m}(\theta_0)\\
 &\leq\frac1M\sum_{v=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^{J_m}2^{-j}\epsilon_m
 \leq\epsilon_m.
 \end{split}
 \tag{21}
\]
Since \(\underline D_{G,m}\leq\widehat D_{G,m}\), (18) includes the true
graph.  Bound (20) is distribution-free and the argument did not depend on
the particular \(G\), \(P\), or \(\theta_0\).  Therefore
\[
 \inf_{G\in\mathcal F}\inf_{P\in K_G}
 \Pr_P\{G\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_m\}\geq1-\alpha.
 \tag{22}
\]

Finally fix \(\delta>0\).  Define the truncated population discrepancy by
\[
 d_J(P,Q)=\frac1M\sum_{v=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^{J}2^{-j}
 |\phi_{P_v}(t_{k_v,j})-\phi_{Q_v}(t_{k_v,j})|.
\]
Its empirical counterpart, with data sampled from \(P\), is
\[
 \widehat d_J(P,Q)=\frac1M\sum_{v=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^{J}2^{-j}
 |\widehat\phi_{v,j}-\phi_{Q_v}(t_{k_v,j})|.
\]
Because characteristic functions have modulus at most one, the exact feature
tail is the bound already obtained in (10):
\[
 0\leq d(P,Q)-d_J(P,Q)\leq2^{1-J}.
 \tag{23}
\]
On the event in which the maximum empirical characteristic-function error is
at most \(a\), the triangle inequality and
\(M^{-1}\sum_v\sum_{j\leq J}2^{-j}\leq1\) give, simultaneously for every
candidate law \(Q\),
\[
 \widehat d_J(P,Q)\geq d_J(P,Q)-a
 \geq d(P,Q)-2^{1-J}-a.
 \tag{24}
\]
Consequently, if
\(\inf_{Q\in K_{G'}}d(P,Q)\geq\delta\), then
\[
 \widehat D_{G',m}
 \geq\delta-2^{1-J_m}-a.
 \tag{25}
\]
This conclusion is simultaneous over all \(G'\in\mathcal F\); no union over
parameters or source decompositions is needed.

Take \(a=\delta/8\).  Equation (20) gives the distribution-free bound
\[
 \sup_P\Pr_P\left\{
   \max_{v,j\leq J_m}
   |\widehat\phi_{v,j}-\phi_{P_v}(t_{k_v,j})|>\delta/8
 \right\}
 \leq4MJ_m\exp(-m\delta^2/256),
 \tag{26}
\]
which tends to zero because \(J_m=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\).  Moreover,
\[
 2^{1-J_m}\leq\frac{2}{m+1}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \epsilon_m\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{27}
\]
If \(G'\) is included, (17)--(18) imply
\[
 \widehat D_{G',m}
 \leq\overline D_{G',m}
 \leq\underline D_{G',m}+\eta_{G',m}
 \leq\epsilon_m+\rho_m+\eta_{G',m}
 \leq3\epsilon_m.
 \tag{28}
\]
For all sufficiently large \(m\), (25) with \(a=\delta/8\) is at least
\(3\delta/4\), whereas (28) is strictly smaller than \(3\delta/4\).
Thus on the complement of the event in (26), every graph separated from the
true law by \(\delta\) is excluded.  Taking the supremum over
\(P\in\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal F}K_G\) and using (26) proves
\[
 \sup_{P\in\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal F}K_G}
 \Pr_P\!\left\{\exists G'\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_m:
     \inf_{Q\in K_{G'}}d(P,Q)\geq\delta\right\}
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The proof compares only observable characteristic functions.  Source
separation, overcomplete independent-component recovery, and a
single-observational-law equivalence claim play no role.
